title: Haptic perception
review_question: To provide an extensive overview of the state of the art of human haptic perceptual capabilities, including material and spatial properties, numerosity, illusions, and applications.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Not specified, as this is a narrative review providing an overview of the field.

evidence_base_summary.date_range: References span from 1690 to 2013, with a focus on recent research up to the publication year.

findings.antecedent: physical roughness (sandpaper grit size)
findings.quote: perceived roughness is related to physical roughness by a power function. The exponent of this power function lies around 1.5.

findings.antecedent: surface features smaller than 30 µm
findings.quote: movement is necessary to perceive the roughness of surfaces with features smaller than 30 µm.

findings.antecedent: adapting to vibration with a frequency of 100 Hz
findings.consequent: sensitivity to vibrational component of roughness perception (fine textures)
findings.quote: The vibrational component of roughness perception... can be reduced in sensitivity by adapting to vibration with a frequency of 100 Hz.

findings.antecedent: texture felt just after a smooth texture
findings.consequent: perceived roughness of the same texture
findings.quote: a texture that is felt just after a smooth texture has been felt, feels rougher than the same texture when it is felt after a rough texture has been felt.

findings.antecedent: touching a surface using a rigid probe instead of directly with the fingers
findings.quote: the intensity of the perceived roughness is higher.

findings.antecedent: physical compliance
findings.quote: for compliance perception, the exponent is less than 1, namely 0.8.

findings.antecedent: surface deformation cue (vs. force/displacement ratio cue)
findings.quote: by far the most information is derived from the surface deformation cue

findings.antecedent: heat extraction rate from the skin upon touch
findings.quote: The heat extraction rate can be perceived and used to obtain information about the object's material

findings.antecedent: differences in heat transfer rate
findings.quote: differences in heat transfer rate of approximately 43% can be discriminated.

findings.antecedent: physical friction
findings.quote: A correlation coefficient of 0.85 was measured between physical and perceived friction using four different materials.

findings.antecedent: skin stretch (cutaneous cue)
findings.quote: When the authors introduced skin stretch, perceived friction increased significantly.

findings.antecedent: physical viscosity
findings.quote: a power law was found relating physical to perceived viscosity, with an exponent of 0.43.

findings.antecedent: physical viscosity (highest vs. lowest)
findings.quote: For the highest viscosity... threshold for stirring with a spatula was about 30%... For lower viscosities... this fraction increased up to 100%.

findings.antecedent: inertial force alone (object moved about) vs. gravitational force alone (object held statically)
findings.quote: heaviness based on this inertial force alone is perceived as half of that based on gravitational force alone.

findings.antecedent: contact area of object lying on the hand
findings.quote: the perceived weight of an object lying on the hand depends on the contact area: the smaller the contact area, the larger the perceived weight.

findings.antecedent: smaller object of equal weight
findings.quote: a smaller object of equal weight is perceived as heavier than a larger one.

findings.antecedent: 3D familiar objects
findings.quote: human observers are indeed very well able to recognize quickly and accurately such objects by touch.

findings.antecedent: haptic vs. visual perception of 3D shape
findings.quote: haptics and vision have functionally overlapping (but not necessarily identical) representations of 3D shape.

findings.antecedent: blind observers (early and late blind) vs. blindfolded sighted observers
findings.quote: blind observers... performed better in a haptic discrimination with these 3D shapes than blindfolded observers.

findings.antecedent: blind vs. sighted observers
findings.quote: blind observers gave more objective judgments than sighted observers

findings.antecedent: local slope information (first order) vs. only height information (zeroth order)
findings.quote: slope information was sufficient because the addition of local curvature information did not change or improve the thresholds.

findings.antecedent: cutaneous receptors (palmar side vs. dorsal side)
findings.quote: Performance with the palmar side was significantly better, indicating again that cutaneous receptors play an essential role

findings.antecedent: increasing length of the stimuli
findings.quote: Increasing the length of the stimuli not only causes a decrease of the curvature discrimination threshold

findings.antecedent: increasing length of the stimuli
findings.quote: but it also increases the perceived curvature of the stimulus.

findings.antecedent: spherical object
findings.quote: a spherical object would not feel spherical but ellipsoidal.

findings.antecedent: small objects
findings.quote: The threshold for discrimination of length using this method lies around 1 mm.

findings.quote: This latter method is less accurate than the finger-span method.

findings.antecedent: object shape (wider vs. taller cylindrical glasses, same actual volume)
findings.quote: wider glasses were estimated to have a larger volume than taller glasses, even though their actual volume was the same.

findings.antecedent: explicit instruction to discriminate surface area (instead of volume)
findings.consequent: biases in volume perception (for spheres, cubes, tetrahedrons)
findings.quote: when participants were explicitly instructed to discriminate the surface area... the biases almost disappeared.

findings.antecedent: salient object properties (e.g., maximum distance between vertex points for wire frames)
findings.quote: salient object properties have a large influence in haptic perception of volume.

findings.antecedent: two bars perceived as haptically parallel
findings.quote: for two bars to be perceived as haptically parallel, the right bar has to be rotated clockwise with respect to the left bar

findings.antecedent: time delay between touching the reference and test bars
findings.quote: a delay between touching the reference and test bars counterintuitively reduces the deviations.

findings.antecedent: non-informative vision (allowed to look around room, not stimuli)
findings.quote: when participants are not blindfolded, but are allowed to look around in the experimentation room... their performance improves.

findings.antecedent: prescribed hand orientation
findings.quote: by rotating the orientation of the egocentric hand reference frame, the size of the deviations can be manipulated.

findings.antecedent: cardinal (horizontal and vertical) vs. oblique orientations
findings.consequent: performance in matching or discrimination tasks
findings.quote: performance is better with cardinal (i.e. horizontal and vertical) orientations than with oblique orientations.

findings.antecedent: haptic oblique effect
findings.quote: They conclude that the haptic oblique effect originates at a high level in the brain.

findings.antecedent: angles (e.g., 90° reference)
findings.quote: the discrimination threshold (75% correct) was 4.7°.

findings.antecedent: small number of items (up to three)
findings.quote: subitizing also occurs in touch.

findings.antecedent: subitizing
findings.quote: The finding that subitizing not only occurs in vision, but also in tactile and haptic perception suggests that this is a modality-independent process.

findings.antecedent: Müller-Lyer illusion stimuli (tactual)
findings.quote: the tactual illusion was even stronger than for vision.

findings.antecedent: Poggendorff illusion stimuli (tactual)
findings.quote: the left line segment seems to be shifted upwards... This inversion was also found by Lucca et al.93 However, Wenderoth and Alais argue that this outcome is an artifact of the method used.

findings.antecedent: adaptation to a curved edge (e.g., 3 minutes)
findings.consequent: perceived curvature of a subsequent straight edge
findings.quote: Most of them commented that the straight edge felt curved in a direction opposite to that of the adaptation curvature.

findings.antecedent: active exploration of a curved surface with index finger (curvature after-effect)
findings.quote: if a curved surface is actively explored with the index finger, the after-effect also transfers to the other hand

findings.antecedent: prior exposure to hot/cold water
findings.quote: the water will feel cold to the hand first exposed to hot water and warm to the other.

findings.antecedent: grill consisting of alternating warm and cold bars (non-painful temperatures)
findings.quote: not an average or intermediate temperature is perceived, but a rather painful sensation of strong heat.

findings.antecedent: number of brief pulses given at only three different locations (e.g., near wrist, arm, further arm)
findings.quote: This stimulation was perceived as a smooth progression of taps on the arm.

synthesis_conclusions: Humans are able to haptically perceive a wide variety of material properties (roughness, compliance, viscosity, friction, coldness) and spatial properties (shape, curvature, size, orientation).
The limits of haptic perception, presented as discrimination thresholds or matching performance, are often quite low, demonstrating the sensitivity of human touch.
Humans assess haptic properties using a set of stereotypical movement patterns, such as lateral motion for texture, unsupported holding for weight, and enclosure for size.
Humans can judge the number of items in their hand, subitizing for small numbers (up to three) rapidly and error-free, and counting for larger numbers.
Touch is susceptible to illusions, similar to vision, including misperceptions of parallelity, volume, weight, curvature after-effects, temperature, and the cutaneous rabbit illusion.
Knowledge of haptic perception is increasingly important for the development of haptic devices and applications like telesurgery and remote sensing.
Haptic research is gaining attention from other perception researchers, often in combination with multimodal perception, leading to rapid expansion of fundamental knowledge about the haptic system.
evidence_gaps: The existence and direction of the tactual Poggendorff illusion remains to be resolved.
limitations: Not explicitly stated for the review itself, but gaps in the literature are identified.

paper_metadata.title: Haptic perception.
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract:
AbstractFueled by novel applications, interest in haptic perception is growing. This paper provides an overview of the state of the art of a number of important aspects of haptic perception. By means of touch we can not only perceive quite different material properties, such as roughness, compliance, friction, coldness and slipperiness, but we can also perceive spatial properties, such as shape, curvature, size and orientation. Moreover, the number of objects we have in our hand can be determined, either by counting or subitizing. All these aspects will be presented and discussed in this paper. Although our intuition tells us that touch provides us with veridical information about our environment, the existence of prominent haptic illusions will show otherwise. Knowledge about haptic perception is interesting from a fundamental viewpoint, but it also is of eminent importance in the technological development of haptic devices. At the end of this paper, a few recent applications will be presented. WIREs Cogn Sci 2013, 4:357–374. DOI: 10.1002/wcs.1238This article is categorized under:

Psychology > Perception and Psychophysics
